newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Fireworks herald Hong Kong's coming handover.
newsitem.headline: Fireworks herald Hong Kong's coming handover.

text.p: Hong Kong brought its Chinese New Year festivities to their official close on Saturday with a spectacular fireworks display, but with a sober thought for the accident during Friday's parade that killed a British tourist.

People began gathering as much as six hours early for the HK$8 million (US$ 1.03 million) extravaganza involving 22,000 rockets fired from five barges in Hong Kong's harbour, the last before the British colony reverts to China later this year.
"I wanted to come because this is 1997," said a photography enthusiast at the waterfront. "And also because this is the first time the display includes a laser show."

The 23 minute show ended with a segment meant to welcome Hong Kong's return to the motherland, and television commentators noted that the territory's next fireworks display was likely to be one marking the handover at midnight of June 30.

Elsewhere during the new year's second day, markets began reopening to let residents buy the makings of traditional new year's meals, decorating fish tanks and vegetable displays with oranges and red paper symbolising prosperity and good luck.

Many also headed to the Che Kung temple commemorating an ancient general and guardian of good health whose birthday is the new year's second day, but gathering crowds made some worry about accidents like the one that marred a parade on Friday.
"I wouldn't bring my children here," one worshipper at the Che Kung temple in Shatin district told local television. "It's too difficult to look after them in the crowd."
Brenda Ann Stevens, 45, of Yorkshire was killed when a float in a New Year parade went out of control on Friday.
Hospital authorities said the driver had a high level of carbon monoxide in his blood when admitted to hospital. Media reports have indicated he may have been overcome by fumes.
"The carbon monoxide level in his blood on admission was very high, around five times the normal level," said Lily Chiu, deputy chief executive of Queen Elizabeth Hospital.
"He actually spoke to our doctors on admission. He told us about his feeling not well during the incident and he was very upset about the accident," she said.

Hong Kong police are arranging to fly in Stevens' next of kin to identify the body, while the vehicle has been impounded and would be examined by government transport experts next week after the holidays, a police spokeswoman said on Saturday.
Some 31 people were also injured in the accident, of whom six remain in hospital. One is still in poor condition, while the others are listed as stable or satisfactory.
